title: The Uman Encirclement
subtitle: The southern campaign and the armies inside the pocket
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: The Uman pocket, Soviet breakout attempts, participating German and Soviet formations and prisoners of war.
body:
At three in the morning on 6 August 1941, a message from the Soviet 12th Army was received describing the position of the 6th and 12th Armies near Podvysokoye, north of Pervomaysk. The armies were encircled, ammunition and fuel were exhausted, and the space they occupied was contracting under fire. Headquarters reported twenty thousand bayonets available and an intention to strike south toward Pervomaysk to join the 18th Army. It requested air attacks against German positions, ammunition deliveries, and the signals needed to coordinate with aircraft. The message combined an operational plan with an inventory of the conditions making that plan increasingly difficult to execute. [1] By 6 August the Uman encirclement had reduced the Soviet armies’ freedom of action to a shrinking set of routes and requests for assistance. Fighting and breakout attempts nevertheless continued beyond that date. The chapter traces how withdrawal became entrapment through the interaction of German manoeuvre, Soviet command decisions and the disappearance of transport connections. It then follows the divergence between the operational result and the subsequent lives of prisoners and civilians. A battle’s closing phase could end an army’s organised resistance while beginning a longer history of captivity, persecution or escape for the people within the defeated formation’s area.

The southern advance changes direction

Army Group South, commanded by Rundstedt, had advanced more slowly than the German formations on the central axis during the invasion’s opening weeks. Soviet resistance and counterattacks imposed substantial demands, while the geography of Ukraine offered several objectives that could not all be pursued by the same force at once. Kiev, the Dnieper crossings, the Soviet armies farther west, and the communications toward the Black Sea were related but distinct problems. The German operation that developed around Uman sought to destroy Soviet forces west of the Dnieper before they could withdraw into a new defensive position. [2] Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group supplied the mobile arm of this operation. After the July advance into the region west of Kiev, its movement turned south and southeast, threatening the rear of Soviet armies retreating from the west. Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army advanced from that western direction toward the area between Uman and Pervomaysk. The combination mattered: the mobile force could reach behind the Soviet troops, while the infantry army pressed them toward the narrowing space. Neither the direction nor the result should be confused with Guderian’s later movement south from Army Group Centre, which belongs to a subsequent stage of the campaign. [2] [3] Muzychenko’s 6th Army and Ponedelin’s 12th Army needed more than permission to move east. Their withdrawal required routes that would remain accessible long enough for infantry, guns, transport and wounded men to pass, together with a receiving position connected to neighbouring forces. German mobile formations sought to seize those connections while pressure from the west prevented an orderly disengagement. The time between issuing an instruction and completing the movement became decisive. A route available to headquarters when it planned the withdrawal could be lost before the last formations reached it, leaving successive parts of the army in increasingly different situations. The 26th Army’s order of 26 July illustrates the widening separation. Its commander, Fyodor Kostenko, assigned defensive positions and local counterattacks after German tank and motorised infantry groups had pressed its formations back. The order identified the 6th Army on its left but stated that there was no tactical contact with it. That single admission is more revealing than a continuous coloured line across a campaign map. The armies remained neighbours in the command’s geographical description, yet their formations were no longer necessarily connected on the ground. [4]

A transfer of command during retreat

On 25 July, Budenny’s Southwestern Direction headquarters ordered the 6th and 12th Armies transferred from Southwestern Front to Southern Front, effective at 20:00. The receiving command was to begin bringing them out of encirclement after dark toward the Zvenigorodka–Talnoye–Khristinovka line and establish a firm defence. The wording demonstrates that the danger was recognised before the final pocket formed. It also shows that withdrawal was authorised; the history cannot accurately be reduced to an absolute prohibition on retreat from beginning to end. The crucial questions concern direction, timing, available routes, and whether orders corresponded to the actual situation. [5] The transfer placed the armies under Tyulenev’s Southern Front while Budenny retained responsibility for the wider southwestern direction. To become effective, the new relationship required reliable information about locations, strength, existing instructions and supply arrangements. The directive’s demands for acknowledgement, reports on orders issued and confirmation of handover addressed those requirements. Administrative procedure was therefore part of restoring operational control during retreat. The transfer offered a basis for coordination with forces to the south, but its value depended on completing that work while the German advance was altering the situation the receiving headquarters had to understand. [5] To the south, the 18th Army confronted the same developing danger from another direction. At 14:00 on 31 July, its commander, Andrei Smirnov, reported measures against the German grouping near Golovanevsk. He asked that Muzychenko attack toward a line including Ladyzhinka and neighbouring settlements, while requesting at least a division from the front reserve to cover the Sinyukha River and secure the rear of three armies. The report warned that without this stabilisation their combined actions would not overcome the enemy penetration. It was an appeal for coordinated action and a defensive safeguard, rather than evidence that either had already been achieved. [6] Smirnov proposed using the 169th Rifle Division against the Golovanevsk threat while other troops held the army’s position. His request reveals the competing functions imposed on limited forces. The same army needed to attack northward, retain its own front, and avoid being cut off from the east. A relief operation could not be detached from those requirements. If the 18th Army itself withdrew south, the distance separating it from the threatened armies would increase. By early August, that was precisely the problem the higher command was forced to acknowledge. [6]

The routes close around the armies

The 26th Army’s defensive arrangements show how commanders tried to deal with penetration when continuous contact had been lost. Its 116th Rifle Division was ordered to send two battalion-sized blocking detachments by truck, provided with antitank artillery, toward threatened roads farther south. Another division was to protect its southern flank with a blocking force near Lisyanka and reconnoitre toward Zvenigorodka. These were attempts to restore information and place obstacles on routes the enemy might exploit. They did not amount to a restored link with the 6th Army. Moving a battalion quickly could cover a road temporarily, but holding a broader interval required infantry, artillery, communications, and reserves that the command still had to assemble. [4] The planned night relief of cavalry by rifle troops illustrates the sequence needed to release a mobile reserve. The incoming force had to reach and assume the position before the departing formation could concentrate for another task. In a threatened sector, shortening that interval risked exposing the line; extending it delayed the reserve’s availability. Around Uman, such competing demands accumulated while German forces closed the roads on which Soviet movement depended. The defeat developed through that interaction between enemy action and the time required for ordinary military processes. No single order can adequately explain the different stages through which the armies lost their remaining options. [4] Uman lay north of the final concentration of trapped troops. The battle’s name should not obscure its shifting geography: Podvysokoye and the wooded area known as Zelenaya Brama became central to the last Soviet resistance, while Pervomaysk lay farther south at an important river junction. The Sinyukha, flowing toward the Southern Bug, formed an obstacle on the eastern side of the threatened area. Rivers that might have supported a new defensive position became barriers to escape when their crossings were held or covered by German forces. A retreating column needed a route for guns and vehicles as well as a passage for individual soldiers. [1] [2] Accounts assign different dates to the closing of the encirclement, partly because initial contacts, the consolidation of the ring, and the ending of organised resistance were separate events. The German Historical Museum’s account places the junction southeast of Uman on 3 August and dates the principal fighting through 8 August. The contemporary Soviet report of 4 August confirms that the German force coming through Zvenigorodka had joined troops advancing from the west. These records support an encirclement consolidated in the opening days of August, while providing no justification for treating every possible exit as sealed at one precisely established hour. [7] [8] Budenny’s report to Stalin on 4 August described the broader consequences with unusual clarity. The 18th Army was withdrawing south and sharply widening the gap separating it from the encircled armies. German forces threatened Southern Front’s right flank and rear across a broad stretch from Kirovograd to Pervomaysk. Mobile reserves were needed, but none were available; newly forming divisions were unready and far from the decisive area. Thus the defeat was not confined to the shrinking pocket. Its development was forcing the command to reconsider the survival and movement of the rest of Southern Front. [8] The same report identified limits to the proposed Soviet response. Counterattacks from the Kiev and Kanev areas could not be synchronised before approximately 10–12 August because forces were still concentrating. Budenny sought to accelerate the Kanev effort to 6–7 August, but doubted that the newly assembled divisions could do more than temporarily divert German attention. Their combat cohesion was inadequate, and the enemy was strengthening in the sector. This was a candid distinction between a desirable operational result and the smaller effect the available force might produce. The trapped armies, meanwhile, could not wait indefinitely for the concentration to finish. [8]

The shrinking resources of 6 August

The twenty thousand bayonets reported at 03:00 described an estimate of infantry fighting strength at that moment. It did not enumerate every person in the pocket. Headquarters staff, artillerymen, transport personnel and wounded soldiers could be present outside the category, while subsequent capture returns covered a wider operation and interval. The distinction changes how the final battle should be understood: the command was measuring the force available to attempt a breakout, alongside a larger population dependent on its success. The number is valuable when read as part of that operational calculation, with its date and scope retained. [1] The proposed movement south also required a rearguard facing north. Even at this late stage, the command was attempting to organise a military withdrawal, with part of the force covering the movement of the rest. That arrangement created a terrible practical difficulty. Troops assigned to hold back the enemy needed ammunition and a later opportunity to disengage; the main force needed enough strength to break through another part of the ring. The report’s inventory of shortages indicates how little freedom remained to satisfy both demands. The plan depended on external assistance that the army urgently requested but could not itself provide. Ponedelin’s brief report on the night attack stated that it had failed and that fighting continued. He asked for bombing at Ternovka. Another message, from military council member Kulikov, requested urgent attacks at Ternovka and Pokotilovo; it was marked as received at 13:25 on 6 August. A later endorsement stated that available aviation had been directed there. The endorsement records a command response, but it does not by itself establish the number of aircraft arriving, the bombs delivered, or the effect on the ground. These distinctions are essential when reconstructing whether a trapped force actually received the support its messages requested. [9] [10] The requests continued into plans for the following night. The 12th Army staff asked for systematic bombing around a list of settlements on the encirclement perimeter during 6 August and the night of 6–7 August. Southern Front staff identified the message as a radio interception and instructed its aviation command to organise night attacks. The survival of this exchange shows that information could still pass out of the pocket, but through imperfect channels. It also establishes that fighting was expected to continue beyond the chapter’s anchor date. A narrative that ends the battle on 6 August would contradict the defenders’ own dated operational messages. [11]

The space needed for liaison

No safe place for a messenger

In a message marked received at 14:20 on 6 August, Ponedelin stated that he could not accept a liaison delegate because there was no suitable territory and a parachutist would be shot. The surviving telegram does not identify a particular messenger or establish that anyone attempted the descent. It records the commander’s assessment of the remaining space. A method intended to repair communications now depended on a protected arrival area that he believed he could not provide. The message gives a sharply bounded indication of how the encirclement impaired command, alongside the better-known shortages of ammunition and fuel.

[12]

Air support and the evacuation problem

The army’s requests for ammunition by air illustrate the final contraction of its supply system. Ordinary deliveries required roads, crossings, and receiving points that were no longer secure. Aircraft offered a possible alternative, but the receiving troops needed to identify themselves and recover loads under fire. The 03:00 message specifically asked for coordination signals, showing that this procedure could not be assumed. Delivering ammunition was a separate task from bombing the enemy, and neither could be inferred simply from the existence of Soviet aircraft elsewhere in the theatre. [1] Budenny had already warned on 4 August that aviation was the principal force still contesting the German outflanking movement, but that it was insufficient. Three reinforcing air regiments had not arrived, and rainy weather since 1 August had sharply restricted operations. This places a documented weather limitation at a specific point in the battle. It also exposes the difference between reinforcement allocated and reinforcement available. An army awaiting support gained nothing immediately from an air regiment still en route, and a regiment that arrived could still face weather and basing constraints. [8] For wounded soldiers, a possible route out had to be usable by the people and transport capable of carrying them. Shortages of fuel and the contraction of defended space therefore affected them differently from fit troops attempting to escape in small groups. The final messages establish those constraints without providing a dependable total of wounded men remaining. Their experience cannot be reconstructed by subtracting one army-strength figure from a later prisoner total. The narrower conclusion is consequential enough: the conditions permitting some soldiers to leave did not ensure the evacuation of those dependent on vehicles, attendants or a more protected passage. The encircling forces retained access to routes outside the pocket and could concentrate pressure against an opponent with diminishing room to manoeuvre. Soviet troops faced increasing difficulty in dispersing, replenishing and assembling for another attempt to break through. German forces still had to maintain the ring and respond to local attacks, but the relationship between their resources and those of the defenders had become increasingly unequal. This explains why continuing resistance could coexist with rapidly declining prospects. The final messages record deliberate efforts to act within a material situation progressively removing the means of carrying those efforts through.

Prisoners and the uses of defeat

The principal battle continued through 8 August in the German Historical Museum’s chronology. More than one hundred thousand Soviet prisoners is the broad figure given in both its account and the U.S. Army synthesis. That figure describes the outcome of the larger operation, not a verified count of captives already assembled on 6 August. Nor should it be treated as a total of soldiers killed. Captured men, dead men, wounded men, and troops who escaped belong to different categories, even when wartime reporting blurred their boundaries. [7] [2] The US Holocaust Memorial Museum’s photograph dated 14 August records a German soldier guarding Soviet prisoners at Uman after the main fighting. It documents a moment in custody rather than providing a count of the camp’s population or deaths. Placed beside the operational record, it marks the transition from the destruction of military organisations to the captors’ authority over individuals. Their removal from an army’s effective strength began a new set of decisions about food, shelter, labour and treatment. Responsibility for those decisions belongs to the institutions exercising custody, whose policies require examination beyond the battlefield’s final returns. [13] German treatment of Soviet prisoners was shaped by racial and political policy, not simply by an overwhelmed supply system. Prisoners received grossly inadequate food and shelter, and selected categories were handed over for killing. In July, arrangements permitted security personnel to screen captives for political and racial persecution, including Jewish prisoners. Logistical difficulties affected the practical conditions of custody, but they do not absolve the authorities that established discriminatory priorities and lethal policies. Later mass mortality must be dated to its actual period rather than compressed into the Uman battle itself. [14] The captured commanders also became objects of competing propaganda. Kateryna Moskalchuk and Oleksandr Chornyi’s study of photographs of Muzychenko, Ponedelin, and Kirillov shows how captivity was used in German publicity and Soviet accusations. Their analysis challenges claims that the images demonstrate voluntary betrayal; it identifies commanders still wearing Soviet uniforms and distinguishes separate photographic sessions. Ponedelin and Kirillov were later executed after their return to the Soviet Union and subsequently rehabilitated. Those later events should not determine the interpretation of every decision they made in the battle, but they explain why the documentary evidence must be separated from accusations constructed after defeat. [15]

Civilians in the battlefield and the occupied town

The military collapse also changed the position of Uman’s inhabitants and those living along the armies’ routes. The closing of a road affected refugees as well as soldiers; the presence of troops increased demands for transport, food, and shelter; and the movement of the front exposed residents to new authorities. These consequences were not experienced uniformly. Jewish residents faced persecution directed at their identity, while other civilians encountered occupation through requisition, labour demands, violence, and the destruction or interruption of ordinary livelihoods. An army-level account must leave room for these different experiences without assigning a single response to an entire population. Evidence associated with postwar proceedings against Günther Herrmann, the former commander of Sonderkommando 4b of Einsatzgruppe C, places the murder of approximately one hundred Jews at a gravel pit in or near Uman in early August 1941. The Yad Vashem account, reproduced in dekoder’s historical mapping project, does not provide a precise day. It supports the presence of organised anti-Jewish killing at the beginning of occupation, without requiring the atlas to date it specifically to 6 August. The perpetrators and the evidentiary basis can be identified even where the chronology remains approximate. [16] The distinction between the early-August murder and Uman’s later massacres allows the development of occupation violence to be traced. Different moments involved particular institutions, victims and remaining opportunities for escape or assistance. Residents encountered those changes without knowing the complete sequence that later research can reconstruct. Their choices were shaped by information, family obligations, health and available routes. Preserving the chronology therefore gives greater precision to responsibility while restoring contingency to civilian experience. It prevents a later outcome from making the preceding choices appear either inevitable or fully informed.

Buzia Leibovych’s later escape

The National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War preserves an account of Buzia Leibovych, a young Jewish woman from Uman who eventually escaped after imprisonment in several labour camps. Her parents and sister had been killed. She sought help from the Boius family in Rosishky and was hidden until the area’s liberation in March 1944. This rescue occurred later in the occupation, not during the encirclement on 6 August. It belongs here as a brief indication of the civilian history that followed the battle. A town’s capture opened a prolonged struggle for survival, involving concealment, dependence on another household, and the loss of family. The museum account supplies that history without requiring an invented scene of what Buzia was doing on the day the armies’ final messages were sent. [17]

What the victory opened, and what it left unresolved

The Uman defeat widened German opportunities toward the lower Dnieper and the Black Sea. It also forced Soviet leaders to distinguish between positions they hoped to retain and forces they could still save. Budenny’s report of 4 August proposed withdrawing Southern Front toward the Ingul and Nikolaev while assigning Odessa’s defence to the Separate Coastal Army. He requested that the Black Sea Fleet organise and protect maritime communications. The proposal linked a land withdrawal to continued resistance at a port supplied by sea, anticipating a different operational problem from the one that had destroyed the armies near Uman. [8] The same report described long stretches of the Dnieper as inadequately covered and proposed moving newly forming divisions before their preparation was complete. It named formations for sectors around Kremenchug, Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, and Nikopol, while acknowledging that some had no established readiness date. This was the wider cost of the defeat. The Soviet command had to rebuild a front with formations whose limitations were known, because waiting for complete preparation risked leaving essential crossings unprotected. German success created new objectives; Soviet survival depended on assembling another defence quickly enough to contest them. [8] For Britain and the United States, the southern crisis formed part of the uncertain military situation in which assistance to the Soviet Union was being arranged. Hopkins’s discussion with Stalin on 31 July had concerned equipment, transport routes, and a war extending into the following spring. It did not promise an intervention capable of rescuing the armies at Uman. The distinction between future coalition strength and immediate battlefield resources remains essential. On 6 August, Ponedelin’s men depended on the forces, ammunition, aircraft, and routes then within reach. [18] Uman destroyed a major Soviet grouping and widened the opportunities available to Army Group South. Its consequences also redistributed the demands of resistance: Soviet headquarters had to cover new river sectors with incompletely prepared formations, while Odessa was assigned a defence dependent on maritime support. Prisoners and civilians entered histories governed by captivity and occupation as well as by the movement of armies. The [12 August chapter](/articles/barbarossa-the-war-widens-1941-08-12) follows the widening operations at Luga, Staraya Russa and Odessa, examining how success in one sector altered the forces and responsibilities available elsewhere.

sourceMethod: Unpublished review draft. Numbered references link to the bibliography and return to their first use. Specific document, paragraph and page locators accompany the references. Soviet military records were read in Russian transcription from the published General Staff collections; English descriptions are paraphrases by the atlas, and archival identifiers are those printed in the collections, not claims of direct archival inspection. Orders establish intentions; situation reports contain contemporary information, estimates and gaps. U.S. Army retrospective studies are read critically alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Publisher excerpts are cited only for inspected passages. Testimony is distinguished from contemporary reporting. Dates in titles anchor the chronology; subsequent developments are dated explicitly. The atlas layers are qualified regional interpretations; their boundaries and arrows are not independent evidence of exact control or unit positions.
